summary: Native nonlinear qubit-readout couplings like cosine-cosine interactions promise intrinsic Purcell protection and suppression of drive-induced leakage through selection rules, but when realized via auxiliary mediator modes, these couplings reintroduce dense multiphoton resonance landscapes and remain highly sensitive to readout frequency. Experiments on a dimon device demonstrate that readout-induced leakage varies by more than an order of magnitude across a ~7% readout frequency window, showing that engineering such couplings requires careful spectral placement of auxiliary modes and elimination of parasitic electromagnetic modes.
motivation: Drive-induced transitions into leakage states limit readout power and speed in superconducting qubits while generating correlated errors harmful to quantum error correction. Understanding whether nonlinear couplings actually suppress these unwanted processes in realistic multimode circuits is critical for designing fast, high-fidelity readout.
method: Floquet steady-state simulations compared ideal and mediated cosine-cosine couplings against linear and balanced cross-Kerr schemes. Pump-probe spectroscopy on a dimon device characterized drive-induced unwanted state transitions across 4–9 GHz; leakage benchmarking measured correlation decay in repeated readout sequences to extract leakage and seepage rates per readout ($L_↑$ and $L_↓$) at two readout frequencies differing by <7% (7.513 GHz and 7.025 GHz).
result: The ideal cosine-cosine interaction shows the sparsest multiphoton resonance landscape, but mediated implementations suffer from resonances reintroduced by the auxiliary mode with frequencies $ω_m/2π ≈ 4.605$ GHz and anharmonicity $α_m/2π ≈ -110.4$ MHz. Between Exp 1 and Exp 2, leakage rates dropped from 2.1% to 0.1% at $\bar{n}_r = 4.9$ photons and 6.3% to 0.1% at $\bar{n}_r = 7.6$ photons, while readout fidelities remained ~99.5–99.7%, demonstrating orders-of-magnitude frequency sensitivity.
